raw_response:
It's October now, and the maize is just coming off the field. I need to get the wheat in the ground within the next week or the window closes. I've got 4.1 mu — not much, but it's what my family has, and every decision matters because there are seven of us to feed.

I'm 33, finished middle school, and I've been farming this land for eight years since my father stepped back. Having middle school means I can read the extension leaflets and I understand what the county technician means when he talks about nitrogen rates and split applications, but I still trust my eyes more than his numbers. The technician says I should target 18 kg of nitrogen per mu for wheat, but three years ago I did 18 and last year I cut back to 15, and the yield difference was maybe 20 kg per mu — not worth the extra 60 yuan in fertilizer. My neighbor Liu Wei, he's about my age, puts down 20 kg and swears by it, but his soil is better and he buys in bulk on 8 mu. I stick with 15 kg for wheat and 14 kg for maize.

My household is full — my parents live with us, my wife, our two kids, and my younger brother who works at a factory in Handan. My brother sends money home, but I don't touch it for the farm. This land is my responsibility. My father helps when his knees allow, and my wife works the fields with me. We don't hire labor. At 150 yuan a day, one worker would eat half my fertilizer budget for an entire mu. With some family working off-farm, our labor is tight during peak times, but on 4.1 mu we manage.

I grow cotton, maize, and wheat — or at least I know cotton. My uncle talked me into planting cotton about five years ago, and I learned my lesson. The picking labor was enormous, the bollworm was a nightmare, and the price dropped that autumn. I tore it out and went back to wheat-maize double cropping. Grain is insurance. Cotton is a gamble I can't afford on 4.1 mu.

For this year's wheat, I'm planting in mid-October right after the maize comes off. I buy improved seed from the county supply store at 35 yuan per mu — I used to save seed, but after two years the vigor drops and you lose more than you save. Before planting, I spread about 25 kg of compound fertilizer per mu and work it in with the rotary tiller. Then at jointing in late March, I watch the color. If it looks pale or yellow, I topdress with 10–12 kg of urea per mu. I never skip the topdress. In 2019 I tried to save money, the spring turned dry, and I lost maybe 80 kg per mu. That hurt. I irrigate three times for wheat — after planting if it's dry, at jointing, and at grain filling. The electricity for the well pump is expensive, about 30–40 yuan each time for my whole plot, but wheat pays the bills.

For maize, the window between wheat harvest and planting is brutal — sometimes only two days if rain is coming. I use hybrid seed, 60 yuan per mu, bought fresh every year because you can't save hybrid seed. All the fertilizer goes in at planting — about 30 kg of compound fertilizer plus a little urea in the furrow. No time for split application. I irrigate twice if the summer is dry, but I don't push it because the summer rains usually help and maize prices aren't great right now. I use herbicide on both crops, and I always add insecticide on the maize because the corn borer was terrible two years ago and I lost ears.

My total input costs this year are about 980 yuan. That's a lot of money for a small plot — it's nearly two months of my brother's wages — but I would rather spend it than risk a disaster. I keep a small cash reserve for emergencies. Last year my daughter needed medicine and the clinic wanted payment upfront. So I don't optimize for maximum yield. I aim for stable, good enough. I expect about 430 kg per mu of wheat and 470 kg per mu of maize if the weather holds.
